yajayācayatavicharakṣonaṅ (gloss: made; artificial). "From yaja, yāca, yat, vicha and rakṣa, naṅ." After yaja and these others, naṅ comes in the sense of the action and so on: pajñaḥ, yācñā, yatnaḥ, viśnaḥ, rakṣṇaḥ.

upasargegtoḥkiḥ. "After a preverb, from ghu, ki." After a preverb, from ghu, ki.

After roots called ghu following a preverb, ki comes: ādiḥ, niṅhiḥ, viṅhiḥ, viṅhiḥ, praṇiṅhiḥ, upaṅhiḥ, pariṅhiḥ.

svaponana. "From svap, nan." After svap, in the sense of the action (gloss: giving age; begging; going; protecting), nan comes: svapnaḥ.

striyāṃktin. "In the feminine, ktin." For the feminine gender too, ktin (gloss: first, or beginning; treasure; permitted; medicine, or; body, or remainder; circumference) comes for the state and for the agent: kṛtiḥ, buṅhiḥ, smṛtiḥ, and so on. Since the commentary says that ni comes after glā, hā, jyā and tvara (gloss: dream): glāniḥ, hāniḥ, jyāniḥ, turṇiḥ. Again, since the commentary explains that ni also comes after what ends in ṝ: kīrṇīḥ, gārṇiḥ, and so on.

ūtiyūtajūti (gloss: skilled; intelligence; mindfulness) sātihetikīrtayaḥ. "Ūti, yūti, jūti, sūhi, heti and kīrti." To av, yu and ju (gloss: exhaustion of joy; empty; aged; swift), by the rule beginning jvaratvara, and to sā, hi and khṝ, kti being added, ūti and these others (gloss: harming; clear) are also set forms (nipātana).

prajayajabhyāṃkyapa. "From vraja and yaja (gloss: protecting; mixed; going; bringing to an end; going; fame), kyap." After vraj and yaj, kyap comes in the sense of the action and so on: vrajyā, ijya (gloss: worship of the gods).

saṃjñāyāṃsamajaniṣadanipatamanavidaṣuñaśiṅbhṛñiṇaḥ. "For a name, from samaja, niṣada, nipata, man, vid, ṣuñ, śīṅ, bhṛñ and iṇ." After samaja and these others, kyap comes for a name and for the state: samajyā, niṣadyā (gloss: going); by pacasvapi and the rest, samprasāraṇa; nipatya, mantā, vadyā, sutyā (gloss: pure), śayyā (gloss: lying down), bhṛtyā (gloss: klarna), ityā (gloss: going).

kṛñośaca. "From kṛñ, śa." After kṛñ, for the state, śa comes. The c serves accent and the ś serves the purpose of śit; for the reason that the ś is marked, yak (gloss: lump; eats for certain); by śayak and the rest it is lengthened (gloss: certainly fallen; pride; knowledge); the augment tuk (gloss: whatever goes); and by the rules giving a and īya: kriyaḥ. Alternatively, kyap being added: krvāṝtyā.

paricaryāparisaryā. "Paricaryā and parisaryā." By adding ya to cara and sṛ preceded by pari, paricarya and parisaryū are set forms.

aḥpratyayāt. "After an affix, a." After roots ending in an affix such as san, a comes (gloss: making): jāgarā, cikīrlā (gloss: making), and so on.

guroścahalaḥ. "And after a heavy syllable, from what ends in a consonant." After a root ending in a consonant that follows the root's heavy first syllable (gloss: serving fully; going fully), a comes for the state: īhā, īkṣā.

ṣiddhvidādibhyo'ṅ. "From those marked with ṣ (gloss: new sleep; wishing to do) and from bhid and the rest, aṅ." After roots marked with ṣ and after bhid and the rest, aṅ comes for the feminine. For those marked with ṣ: mṛjā, jarā, vacā, and so on. For bhid and the rest (gloss: making; looking): bhidā, chidā, vidā, kṣipā, guhā, medhā, and so on.

cintipūjikathikumpicarcaśca. "And from cinti, pūji, kathi, kumbi and carca." After cint and these others, too, aṅ comes for the state (gloss: pure; old woman; cooking woman): cintvā, pūjā, kathā, kumba, carcā (gloss: split; cut; knowledge; desire; secret, or hidden; wise mind).

taścopasarge. "And after āt, with a preverb." After roots ending in ā preceded by a preverb, aṅ also comes: sanṭhṇā, saṃsthā, bradā, and so on.

ṇyasaśranthoyuca (gloss: like the mind; worship; talk; tent; worship). "From ṇi, ās and śrantha, yuc." After roots ending in ṇic, and after ās and śrantha, yuc comes: kāraṇā, āsanā, śrantānā.

pareḥpā. "Optionally after pari" (gloss: holding all; abiding properly; giving thoroughly). After iṣu preceded by pari, yuc optionally comes: paryeṣaṇaḥ. Alternatively, kti being added: parīṣṭiḥ.

ṇvulabahulaṃ. "Ṇvul, variously." For the feminine gender, in the state, the agent and others (gloss: wishing to do; seat; relaxed), ṇvul variously comes: āsikā (gloss: sitting), śāyikā (gloss: lying down), and so on. Since the commentary explains that kāra (gloss: searching fully) comes after letters in their own sense (gloss: in the sense of "fully"; the letter a): ākāraḥ, ikāraḥ, for the vowels, and kakāraḥ, khakāraḥ, gakāraḥ, and so on. Again, since the commentary says that for the letter r, ipha optionally comes: rephaḥ, rakāraḥ.

ajādibhyaḥiñ. "From those beginning with a vowel, iñ." After roots beginning with a vowel, iñ comes for the state and so on (gloss: the letter i): ājiḥ, ādiḥ (gloss: the letter ka, the letter kha, the letter ga), and so on.

vapādibhyaḥiṇ. "From vapa and the rest, iṇ." After vapa and the rest (gloss: the letter r), iṇ comes for the state and so on: vāpi, vāsiḥ, and so on.

kṛṣādibhyaḥik. "From kṛṣ and the rest (gloss: increasing; eating), ik." After kṛṣ and the rest, ik comes for the state: kṛṣiḥ, giriḥ, kariḥ.

vibhāṣākhyānāparipraśnayoriñ. "For narration and for questioning (gloss: sowing seed; dwelling), iñ, optionally." When narration or questioning is to be understood, iñ optionally comes for the feminine state: kātvaṃkāriḥkāmakārṣī. Alternatively, ṇvul being added (gloss: dug; mountain; harming): kātvāṃkāirikākīmakārṣī.

ākrośenañyaniḥ. "For abuse, after nañ, ani." When abuse is to be understood, ani comes after a root preceded by the negative nañ: ajanani, and so on.

lyuṭca. "And lyuṭ as well" (gloss: what work did you do, making the words into chapters?). After a root, in the sense of the action, lyuṭ (gloss: what work did you do, making the words into chapters?) commonly comes, and it is of the neuter gender: jñānaṃ, mānaṃ, pramāṇaṃ, gamanaṃ, bhojanaṃ, and so on.

vāyau. "Optionally, before yu." Before yu, that is, lyuṭ (gloss: unknowing, or unborn), aja optionally becomes vi: vayanaṃ, ajanaṃ.

Cited in the commentary: ṣṭhivuṣivorlyunyupadhādīrghovā. "Of ṣṭhivu and ṣivu, before lyuṭ, the penultimate (gloss: wisdom; respect; great respect; going; food) is optionally lengthened." Before lyuṭ, the penultimate of ṣṭhīvu and ṣivu is optionally lengthened: ṣṭhṭivanaṃ (gloss: casting away), sīvanaṃ (gloss: teaching; increasing). Alternatively, guṇa being applied by the rule on a penultimate light vowel before puk and the rest: ṣṭhevanaṃ (gloss: casting away), sevanaṃ (gloss: teaching).

puṃsisaṃjñāyāṃghaḥ. "In the masculine, for a name, gha."

In the masculine, gha also comes for an action and for a name: pakaḥ, gocaraḥ, sañcaraḥ.

chādeḥghe'dbyupasargasya. "Of chādi before gha, when it does not have two preverbs." Chādi, when no pair of preverbs or the like precedes it, becomes short before gha: bracharaḥ. When there are two preverbs it does not change: samubrachadaḥ.

vahavrajavyajāvaṇanigamāśca. (gloss: tserpa; domain of activity; conduct.) "Vaha, vraja, vyaja, avaṇa and nigama as well." Vaha, to obtain; vraja, to go; vyaja, debt; apa, to pervade; ni with the gamḷ above: gha being applied to these, (gloss: covering) vahaḥ, vrajaḥ, vyajaḥ, apaṇaḥ, (gloss: having grasped, it closely covers) nigamaḥ: these are set forms (nipātana).

khanoghaca. "From khana, gha as well." From khan, in the sense of an action, gha comes, and ghañ also comes: ākhanaḥ, ākhānaḥ.

īṣaduḥsuṣukhala. "When īṣat, dur and su precede, khal." (gloss: obtaining; going; debt; pervading.) To a root following ṣat, dur and su, in the sense of an action, khal comes: īkhatkaraḥ, duḥkaraḥ, sukaraḥ, and so on.

kartṛkarmaṇoścabhūkṛñoḥ. (gloss: digging all around.) "Also from agent and object, for bhū and kṛñ." When īṣat, dur and su come before the agent and object words, khal also comes from bhū and kṛñ following them: īṣadāḍyaṃbhavaṃ, durāḍhyaṃbhavaṃ, (gloss: makes slightly; makes with difficulty; makes easily) svāḍhyaṃbhavaṃ, īṣadāḍhyaṃkaraḥ, durāḍhyaṃkaraḥ, svāḍhyaṃkaraḥ.

ātoyuca. "From ā, yuc." To a root ending in ā, following īṣat, dur and su, in the sense of an action, yuc comes, and mum is not given by the rule on kha and the rest (gloss: becomes slightly rich; becomes rich with joy; becomes rich easily; makes slightly rich; makes rich easily). Khal does not come: īṣatvānaḥ, duḥbānaḥ, supānaḥ.

śāsiyudhidṛśidhṛṣimṛṣibhyaśca. "From śāsi, yudhvi, dṛśi, dhṛṣi and mṛṣi as well." From these, śāsi and the rest, following īṣat, dur and su, yuc also comes: suśāsanaḥ (gloss: well taught), suyodhanaḥ (gloss: fights well; drinks a little; hard to drink; easy to drink), sudarśanaḥ (gloss: sees well), sudharṣaṇaḥ (gloss: drinks well), sumarṣarṣaḥ.

alikhalāoḥpratiṣedhegdā. "From alaṃ and khalu, in prohibition, ktvā." When alaṃ and khalu are used in the sense of prohibition, khvā comes: alaṃkṛtvā, khalukṛtvā.

samānakartṛkayopūrvyākyāle. "For those with the same agent, at the earlier time." (gloss: endured well, or endured greatly.) Of the actions of the same agent, when the earlier time is expressed, ghā comes: ghukhābrājati, pitvābrajati.

kṣīskandasyandoḥ. "Of skanda and syanda, before ktvā." (gloss: makes ornament; makes certain.) The letter n of skanda and syanda is not elided before ktvā. By "car before khar," and by the rule on jhar before something like jhar, the upper t being dropped: skantvā, syantvā. To syandū, iṭ being optionally given by the rule on roots whose ū goes and the rest: (gloss: goes having eaten; goes having drunk) syanditvā.

mriḍamṛdhagudhakuṣabadavasaḥktvā. "From mṛḍa, mṛdha, guṅha, kuṣa, kliśa, vada and vas, ktvā." The gtvā with iṭ following these, mṛḍ and the rest, also bears the name of one whose k goes (gloss: having dried; having scattered): mṛḍitvā, mṛthitvā, kudhitvā, kuṣṛtvā, kliśaktvā (gloss: sorrow), kliṣḍā (gloss: having scattered). Vad and vas being changed by samprasāraṇa through the rule on vaci, svapi and the rest: uditvā, uṣitvā.

nopadhātvāphāntādvā. "From na as penultimate, from a final tha or pha, optionally." From roots such as śrantha and gunpha, which have the letter n as penultimate (gloss: having gathered; rich; snow frog; having pierced; iṭ being optional by the rule on roots whose u goes and the rest) and have a tha or pha at the end, the ktvā that follows, with iṭ, (gloss: having spoken; having sat) is optionally made to bear the name of one whose k goes: śrathitvā (gloss: from the sūtra, tsepa), śanthitvā, guphitvā, gunpitvā, and so on.

bañciluñcaṛtaśca. "From vañci, luñci and ṛt as well." From vañci, luñci and ṛt as well, the ktvā that follows, with iṭ, optionally bears the name of one whose k goes: bacitvā (gloss: having gone), bañcitvā, lucitvā (gloss: nyepa), luñcitvā, ṛtitvā. With the t dropped by the rule on jhar-like sounds and the rest: ṛtvā (gloss: the Lord; assembly).

tṛṣimṛṣikṛśeḥkāśyapasya. "From tṛṣi, mṛṣi and kṛśi, in the view of Kāśyapa." That the khyā with iṭ following these, tṛṣi and the rest, optionally bears the name of one whose k goes is held by the ancient sage Kāśyapa (gloss: he is said to be the name of the father of the sun (Sūrya); the Lord): traṣitvā, trārṣitvā, mṛṣitvā, marṣitvā, kṛśitvā, karśitvā.

jṝpraścoḥktvī. "From jṝ and vraśca, before ktvā." To the ktvā following jṝ and vraśc, iṭ always comes: jaritvā, vraścitvā.

uditobā. "After one whose ut goes, optionally." To the ktvā following a root whose ut goes, iṭ (gloss: thirst) optionally comes (gloss: patience). For śamu and (gloss: subtle) damu, the iṭ of ktvā being made optional, in the alternative without iṭ, by the rule that turns a nasal-bearing root to ā and the rest, (gloss: having grown old): śamitvā, śātvā (gloss: cutting), damitvā, dātvā.

kramaścaktī. "Of krama also, before ktvā." The penultimate of kram is optionally lengthened before ktvā without iṭ: krāntā, krantā. When there is iṭ it is not lengthened: kramitvā.

pūdaśca. "From pūṅ as well." To the ktvā following pūṅ, iṭ optionally comes: pavitvā (gloss: Śiva), būtvā (gloss: tulga).

jāntanaṃśāṃvibhāṣā. "Of j-finals and naśa, optionally." The letter n of roots ending in j and of niśa is optionally elided before ktā (gloss: legs stretched out): for bhañja, (gloss: legs stretched out) bhaktvā, bhaṃktvā, naṣṭvā, naṃṣṭrā, and so on.

jahāteścahiktvi. "Of jahāti, (gloss: having been cleansed; pure) hi before ktvā." Jahāti, that is, the root called ohāṅ, "to go," becomes hi before ktvā: hitvā.

samāse'nañapūrvektvolyapa. "In a compound not preceded by nañ, lyap for ktvā." (gloss: having entangled; not seen.) Where no compound with nañ precedes, at the end of a compound ktvā becomes lyap; the pa has the special purpose of bringing the augment tuk: prakṛtya. When there is nañ: akṛtvā (gloss: having gone), and so on.

pālyapi. "Optionally before lyap." The elisions of the nasal explained above are made optional before the lyap that replaces ktvā: āgatya, āgamya, praṇatya, and so on.

nalyapi. (gloss: natural form; not made.) "Not before lyap." Before the lyap that replaces ktvā, ghu, mā, sthā and the rest do not change to ī: vidhāya (gloss: holding apart), bradāya (gloss: giving forth), prasthāya (gloss: setting out), and so on. (gloss: entirely.) To mīṅ, (gloss: bowing down) ktvā having become lyap, and the root having changed to ā by the rule on mīnāti and the rest: nīmāya, and so on.

lyapilaghupūrvāt. "Before lyap, after a preceding light syllable." The final of ṇic, when a light syllable precedes it, becomes ay before lyap: ṇica, bigaṇayyaḥ.

bibhāṣāyyaḥ. "Ay optionally." Āpḷ ending in ṇic (gloss: certainly harms) optionally becomes ay before lyap: prābayya, prāpya, the ṇi being dropped where there is no iṭ. Since the commentary explains that kṣi is optionally lengthened before lyap (gloss: wishing to gather fully; wishing to bow down): prakṣiya, prakṣitya.

mayateridanyatarasyāṃ. "Of mayati, it optionally." The ā of mayati, that is, mēṅ, "to harm," (gloss: rabtu jabpa) becomes it before lyap: abamitya, abamāya.

lyapica. "Before lyap as well." Before lyap, peñ does not change to samprasāraṇa (gloss: wholly exhausted): prabāya.

bibhāṣāpare. "After pari, optionally." Before lyap, vyeñ following pari changes to samprasāraṇa (gloss: harms all around): parivīya, parivyāya.

ābhīkṣtyeṇamulca. "In repetition, ṇamul as well." When the earlier action of a single agent takes the qualification of repetition (gloss: continuing on), ktvā comes and ṇamul also comes: bhuktvābhuktvāprajati, bhojaṃbhojaṃprajati, and so on.

karmaṇyaktośekṛñaḥkhamuña. (gloss: rolled up completely.) "When kṛñ is joined with an object, khamuñ." To kṛñ following an object word, when it conveys abuse, khamun comes; the kha is for the sake of mum, and the ña for the sake of vṛddhi: cauraṃkāri. If it is not abuse (gloss: goes having eaten and eaten), ktvā is applied: sādhukṛtvāstauti.

svādumiṇamul. "With 'sweet,' ṇamul." Kṛñ following a word meaning "sweet" takes ṇamul: svādukāraṃbhukte, "having made it sweet, he eats." Or, with ktvā applied, (gloss: does the act of a thief) svādukṛtvāphukte, "having made it sweet, he eats."

anyathibaṃkathamitthaṃbhyaśca. (gloss: having said "Well done!", he praises.) "From anyathā, evaṃ, kathaṃ and itthaṃ as well." Kṛñ following anyathā, kathaṃ, itthaṃ and many others takes ṇamul: anyathākāraṃbhukte, evaṃkāraṃbhukte, kathaṃkāraṃbhukte, itthaṃbhukte, and so on.

jībādvideḥ. "From jīva, from pidi." When vidi is heard following jīva, ṇamul comes: jībavedaḥbhukte.

nimūlasalayoḥkaṣa. "With nimūla and sala, from kaṣa." (gloss: he eats having done it otherwise; he eats having done it thus; he eats having done it how; he eats having done it like this.) From kaṣa following nimūla and sal, ṇamul comes: nimūlalakāṣaṃ, salakāṣaṃ.

śuṣkacūrṇa (gloss: he eats having obtained a living) rukṣeṣupiṣaḥ. "With śuṣka, curṇa and rākṣa, from piṣa." To piṣa following śaṣka, curṇa and rūkṣa, ṇamul comes: śuṣkapeṣaṃ, cūrṇapeṣaṃ, rūkṣabeṣaṃ.

samūlākṛtajīveṣuhanakṛñ (gloss: certainly harms from the root) grahaḥ. "With samula, ākṛta and jīva, from han, kṛñ and graha." From han, kṛñ and graha, following samūla, ākṛta and jīva respectively, (gloss: grinds dry; grinds fine; grinds coarse) ṇamul comes: samūlabhātaṃ, ākṛtakāraṃ, jībagrāhaṃ.

hastakarayoḥbartigrahābhyāṃ. "With hasta and kara, from varti and graha." From varti and graha following hasta and kara, ṇamul comes: hastagrāhaṃ, karagrāhaṃ, hastabartaṃ, karabartaṃ.

svepuṣaḥ. "With sra, (gloss: destroys it from the root; made by acting all around; makes one hold on to life) from buṣa." From puṣa following sva, ṇamul comes: svapoṣaṃ.

upamānekarmaṇica. "In comparison, with an object." In comparison, (gloss: seized with the hand; seized the hand; seized the hand) ṇamul also comes from an agent word and from an object word: ratvānidhāyaṃ.

upadaṃśastṛtīyāṃ. "With the third, from ubadaṃśa." From upadaṃśa following a nearby word that ends in the third case (gloss: self-victor), ṇamul comes: mūlakenobadaṃśabhūṃkte, "he eats, biting along with the root vegetable."

apādāneparīpsāyāṃ. "In the source, in utmost haste." (gloss: from āt, yuk; holds firmly like a jewel.) With a nearby word ending in the source, that is, the fifth case, in the sense of an action that conveys great haste, ṇamul comes: śayāyāḥ (gloss: rose from lying down) utthāyaṃ.

dvitīyāṃca. "With the second as well." From a nearby word ending in the second case as well, when conveying haste, in the sense of an action, ṇamul comes: yaṣṭiṃgrahaṃyudhyanta.

abyayeyathābhibriyākhyānekṛñaḥktrāṇamulau. (gloss: to the tthā preceded by ut, ḍamul, with the augment suk; in ut, dropped by the rule on tthā, mhū and the rest.) "With an indeclinable, in expressing delight, ktvā and ṇamul from kṛñ." From a nearby word that is an indeclinable, (gloss: having seized the staff, they make them fall) for an action that conveys the sense of expressing delight, ktvā and ḍamul come: urcaicakṛtyapriyāṃbrute, uccaikṛtvāpriyāṃprūte, uccaikāraṃpriyīprūte, and so on.

iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sūtrātkṛtādayasāmābhūḥ, that is: here ends kṛt and the rest, from the sūtra of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa.

With these, from The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, which sets down as notes the meaning of the root text and its commentary, the procedures, the illustrative examples and so on, for the great treatise on grammar, the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa (gloss: expressing delight, he raised it high; expressing delight, he raised it high), the main procedures for deriving nouns from roots, kṛt and the rest, with general rules and exceptions, are for the time being complete.

At the end of the commentary there come a colophon and verses of auspicious wishes:

prakṛākaumātīseyi rāmacandraprakāśitā, asatvacastamovartūtācca korabriyāciri.

In Tibetan:

This treatise, the Very Clear,
Was made fully clear by Rāmacandra.
It binds the last of untrue speech,
And ever gladdens the discerning and the noble.

So it is said.

Second, the expression of auspiciousness:

ācārya bātu bhagabāna śiṣyaṃ pātu bināyakaḥ, nirbighīsyācca sarvatra bāṇinīya prasādataḥ.

In Tibetan:

May the Blessed One protect the teacher;
May the Guide protect the disciple.
Through the kindness of the sage Pāṇini,
May there be no obstacle anywhere.

maṅgalaṃ lekhakānāṃ ca bāthakānāṃ ca maṅgalaṃ, maṅgalaṃ sarvabhūgānaṃ bhūmibhūpati maṅgalaṃ.

May the writers be fortunate,
May the readers be fortunate,
May all living creatures be fortunate,
May the land and the lord of the land be fortunate.

So it is said.

Thus, among the eight great treatises on grammar, the one that excels in meaning, procedure and the rest, and is, in short, like the mother of all the sciences of language, is the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa. It was bestowed in person by the noble Lokeśvara upon the great brahmin Pāṇini, whom our Teacher, the peerless King of the Śākyas, prophesied in the Root Tantra of Mañjuśrī and elsewhere. This work, called The Chariot That Draws the Jewel of Excellent Explanation, sets down as notes the meaning, procedures, illustrative examples and so on of its root text and commentary. It came about in this way.

Our peerless refuge and sublime ally, for all of us who dwell among the snow mountains, is the noble Padmapāṇi himself, who has arisen in the form of a vajra-holder endowed with the three vows. For a purpose I mention him by name: the Victorious Lord, the great Omniscient One, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso Jigme Gocha Thubten Langtsö De Tsangse Shepai Dorje. He cared for the paṇḍita brothers with the rays of his peerless compassion, and without effort granted them every requisite they could wish for, including many hundreds of zho of gold and silver. To me, his subject, he also gave this command: "Translate the root text into Tibetan, and set down as notes the meaning and the illustrative examples of the commentary." Through the immeasurable kindness of that holy one, I trained a little in the tradition of grammar.

I am the least of his subjects, born of the Se clan in the region of Dar in Upper Tsang, Ngawang Phuntsok Lhundrub, also named Tsewang Rabten Dorje, a dull and idle Tibetan. In the presence of the brothers, the mahāpaṇḍita Balabhadra, born of a pure brahmin family in Kurukṣetra in the Noble Land and learned in the five fields of knowledge, and the paṇḍita Gokulanātha Miśra, I listened carefully to the derivation of the words of the root text, its meaning, its illustrative examples and so on, and translated the root text into Tibetan.

I took as my basis the commentary composed by the great master Rāmacandra called the Prakriyā, that is, "The Procedure." The procedures that are hard to understand, such as those of the Complete Explanation, I adorned in the margins with the oral tradition of learned masters and expanded somewhat, and those that are easy to understand I kept brief.

I began it on an auspicious day of the waxing moon in the Chutö month, in the male dog year called Nachang, which is reckoned by fire, sky and ocean, and by ten cycles of sixty years with thirty-two mixed in, when I had reached the age of twenty-five. (note: detailed annotations on the derivations of the root text have been added.) I completed it in the iron rat year called Kündén, on the third victory day of the waxing half of the month of Caitra, at the auspicious time of the conjunction of Bashé, in my own quarters, Gyüteng Jilpo, at the great Dharma college of glorious Drepung. May this work, too, benefit the teaching and all sentient beings.

Since my own understanding is still very young, there may be impure translation in this work, or contradictions and errors in the illustrative examples, the meanings and so on. If any appear, I pray that the supreme lamas and the assembly of the learned bear with them patiently and correct them properly.

By this virtue, may the glorious Lord of Speech,
Who holds as his ground the precious gold where all the secrets of dense splendor gather,
The sole friend of the boundless beings to be trained throughout the three realms,
Whose sun and moon of excellent intelligence circle and pervade the vast sky of the knowable,
Who possesses the splendor of knowledge deeper than the ocean, remain firm for as long as there is time.

And may the white parasol of the twofold law, wrought by the good deeds of countless beings,
Adorned with the finial of a wish-fulfilling jewel that grants the splendor of every wish, excellent and vast,
Raised high in the sky, never to be stopped, filled with the cool shade of benefit and happiness,
Dispelling the torment of adversity for the teaching and for beings, become supremely and surpassingly beautiful.

If, in this work, the dust of wrong ideas has clouded
The lovely face of the meaning of the text, so that it is not clear,
I do not hide it before the eyes of the supreme and holy learned;
I pray that you polish it with the three pure examinations.

From the sole father of the Ganges, his way of knowledge,
May the clear, slow-flowing river of excellences that issues forth
Wash away all the stains of ignorance of thinking beings,
And enter the precious ocean of omniscience.

This concludes the translation. The following are translator's notes.

The opening verses are ornate praise in which the names of the author's teachers seem to be woven (for example Ngawang, Kelzang, Gelek, Rinchen Jungné, Padkar), the second and third verse in particular being obscure; they are translated by their surface sense. "Balabhadra" renders སྟོབས་བཟང, taken as the Sanskrit name of the Indian paṇḍita who taught the author; this identification is uncertain. In the Mañjuśrī tantra quotation, དཔང་ཕྱུག is read as དབང་ཕྱུག (Lokeśvara). The master of the Siddhāntakaumudī is spelled བྷ་ཊོ་ཛཾ་བྷ་དྲ in the Tibetan; he is Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. The Kāśikā is attributed here to "Kāśikara," as the text has it. In the commentary on the it rule, the name "possessing intent" (དགོང་པ་དང་བཅས་པ) is translated literally; the Tibetan otherwise renders the term it as "going" (འགྲོ་བ). རྐྱེད is read as རྐྱེན "affix".  Several evident copyists' slips are read: བསཱུ་བ as བསྡུ་བ "collection"; ལྷ་བུ as ལྟ་བུ "like"; དགའ in the vṛddhi rule as དག "both"; ངུར as དུར "dur"; བྲད as བྲང "chest"; ཡྕེ as ལྕེ "tongue". The Tibetan spellings of the Sanskrit sūtras and collection names are kept letter for letter, even where they differ from the standard forms of Pāṇini's text. The gloss list of the twenty prefixes is loosely arranged in the Tibetan; the glosses are assigned to the nearest prefix.  The string of glosses at the start (also, exceedingly past, good, and so on) appears to continue the glosses of the twenty prefixes from the previous piece. Evident copyists' slips read: མེ་ཟད as མི་ཟད "indeclinable"; ཀྱེ as ཀྱི; ཉར as ཧར in the hari example. The line "pen tip here; mchang this; ma this" and the phrase ཞེ་ལོང་ཞིག look like scribal jottings that entered the text; they are rendered literally. The worked examples (dadhi ānaya, madhu atra and so on) are kept exactly as the Tibetan spells them, though several stages are garbled.  This is a Tibetan commentary on Pāṇinian grammar; the sūtras are 6.1.78 to 6.1.91 and related rules and vārttikas. The Sanskrit forms are given in their intended standard spelling; the Tibetan transcriptions are often defective (b for v, dropped or extra letters, e.g. "edhrati," "kṛrṇekatvam," "braśnauhaḥ"). The piece is interspersed with interlinear glosses (meanings of the examples, such as "they said," "the cow here," "the wealth of Kṛṣṇa," "debt of a debt") that have been copied into the running text, often displaced from the example they explain; they are translated where they stand. The verse defining the akṣauhiṇī is likewise displaced into the svaira discussion. Its first word, སུས་འགྱུར, is unclear; it is read as སུམ་འགྱུར, "threefold." In "oneness with Kṛṣṇa," གཉིད is read as ཉིད. The example for ūṭh is read as prasthauhaḥ; the Tibetan transcription is garbled. ཚིག་ཕྲད is taken in the Pāṇinian sense of nipātana, a form set down as given. The Tibetan gloss on upānah ("bound on closely") is rendered as "a sandal bound on the foot"; the syllables following it are unclear. This piece is a set of notes on Pāṇini's grammar in which short Tibetan interlinear glosses on the Sanskrit example words have been run into the main text, often displaced from the word they gloss (for instance the glosses on the feminine forms ajā, eḍakā and so on, and on karttrī, daṇḍinī and so on, appear several words later in the Tibetan). I have placed each gloss beside the word it evidently explains. A few intrusive fragments yield no sense and are not rendered: "having made" and "on" inside the Sanskrit verse, a stray "ma" after udeto, "de phan mi" among the flower compounds, and "dang babs" after the glosses on jyeṣṭhā and so on. This section is technical Pāṇinian grammar, and several words carry their grammatical senses. འགྲོ་བ ("going") renders it, an indicatory letter that drops away, translated here as "marker"; རྐྱེན, elsewhere "condition," here means pratyaya in its sense of suffix, and བར་རྐྱེན is the intermediate suffix (vikaraṇa); sup and tiṅ are the nominal and the verbal endings. The "first, middle and last" persons are the Sanskrit prathama, madhyama and uttama, which correspond to the English third, second and first persons; yuṣmad and asmad are the stems of the pronouns "you" and "I." The Tibetan verse calls nature "king" (here "sovereign"), which the author's gloss reads as the victors, the buddhas. A few evident scribal slips were read in context: the five from laṅ to lṛṅ are read as ṅ-marked (the text has པ for ང), "from ta up to ṅ" reads ཏ་ནས་དའི་ནར as ཏ་ནས་ངའི་བར in line with the later definition of tiṅ, and སྐད་གསང is read as སྐད་གདངས, "pitch," in the description of svarita; where the gloss writes ཏ་ད and དི་ཏ, the terms are taken as taṅ and ṅit, as the explanations that follow show. Technical terms keep their Pāṇinian senses: "marker" renders "going" (it), "suffix" renders rkyen (pratyaya), "pertaining to all roots" and "pertaining to half the roots" are sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka, guṇa is the grammatical strengthening of a vowel, and su, au and jas are the nominative endings. The text uses the Indian order of persons: its first person (prathama) is the Western third person, its middle person the second, and its last person (uttama) the first. The derivations are very terse, and the Tibetan copy has many slips in the Sanskrit forms and in the names of the rules cited; the forms are given in their standard spelling, and the slips are read from the parallel derivations and the rules invoked. In particular, the bracketed yaṅ is read as laṅ, which with laṭ, liṅ and loṭ makes the four lakāras whose endings are sārvadhātuka; andra is read as ant; a phrase repeated in the abhūt derivation is translated once; and in the abhūtam derivation, where only "becomes s" stands, "la becomes thas" is supplied from the following step. The explanation of the gāti rule glosses pā as "to protect," although the line just before glosses it as "to drink," which is how the Pāṇinian tradition takes it here. In the derivation of abhaviṣātām, the closing "ṭ is brought in" does not fit the form and seems to be carried over from the derivation of abhaviṣṭa.  As in the preceding derivations, the Sanskrit forms are given in their standard spelling, and the scribal slips in the steps are read from the parallel derivations and the rules invoked. For instance, the Tibetan rendering of the sūtra on s before dh reads "also before bha," taken as "also before dh," as the rule is cited a little later; the ending written thas in the derivation of abhaviṣṭhāḥ is taken as thās; and in the explanation of the māṅ rule, where the copy reads na yin, the evident ma yin, "does not," is translated, as the rule requires. The two forms that illustrate the option in which s becomes d are transcribed exactly as they stand. The derivation placed under the heading for the last person in fact repeats the case of dhvam, the middle person plural; the last person forms begin with abhaviṣi. The Tibetan glosses of the examples with mā read literally "did not become," although with the prohibitive mā the Sanskrit means "may not become."  As in Indian grammar generally, the "first person" here is what Western grammar calls the third person, the "middle person" is the second, and the "last person" is the first; so babhūva in the first person singular means "he was," and in the last person singular "I was."
The Tibetan of this piece has many scribal slips in its technical terms, which I have translated in their evident reading: laṭ for liṭ in the rule "for what is out of sight, liṭ"; arkus for atus; jñu for jhi; athas for thas; at for a; ā for ū; tha for pa or va; damaged spellings of abhyāsa, of thung ngu ("short"), of snga ma ("the former") and of phyed pa (in the term for ārdhadhātuka); yon for yod ("there is"); zad for med ("no"); and 'phrod, read as 'phros ("remaining"). In the first person dual the text says the v is joined to i; the form requires a, and I have read a.

The three benedictive forms of cikitsa are garbled in the Tibetan (ཙིཀིཏྶཏཧ, ཙི་ཀི་ཏྶ་སྟཱཾ, ཙི་ཀི་ཏྶྟསུཿ) and are rendered as the forms the derivation describes. The phrase ནད་དོ་བར་བྱེད after "before the ārdhadhātuka affixes," and ཐི་ཚོམ་བྱེད ("making doubt") before "the letter ṅ of īyaṅ," are unintelligible in context and are left unrendered. "san and yaṅ" renders ཡང་དག, here the Sanskrit affix yaṅ, not the Tibetan word "genuine." The opening derivation of edhate is terse and partly garbled and is rendered step by step as it stands.  This is a section of a Sanskrit grammatical commentary deriving the ātmanepada forms of the root edh ("to grow") in laṭ, the optative (liṅ), loṭ, laṅ, luṅ and liṭ. The Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit forms and endings is heavily corrupted in this witness (for example ངྷ for dh, ཨེེ for ai, and many garbled syllables); the forms are given here in their evident standard Sanskrit shape, and the grammatical rules, which the Tibetan cites by translating their wording, are rendered according to the Pāṇinian sūtras they plainly reflect (for instance āto ṅitaḥ, lopo vyor vali, liṅaḥ salopo 'nantyasya, jho 'ntaḥ, ato guṇe, savābhyāṃ vāmau, eta ai, āḍ uttamasya pic ca, āḍ ajādīnām, āṭaś ca, ādeśapratyayayoḥ, ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ, ātmanepadeṣv anataḥ, ijādeś ca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ, āmaḥ). This is a section of a Pāṇinian verb-conjugation manual; the "first person" of the Sanskrit grammarians is the English third person. Sanskrit rule-citations and paradigm forms are given in romanized Sanskrit following the Tibetan transliteration (which writes dh as ṅh), keeping its convention of writing final consonants with an inherent a (e.g., avyātsīta, puṣyāta). A few evident copyist's slips in the forms have been given in their intended shape (e.g., abuṣatāṃ for apuṣatāṃ, aśīṣyata for aśliṣyata, piḍhyāsuḥ for vidhyāsuḥ, tṛbyati for tṛpyati, aśleṣyata for aślekṣyata). The reduplicated paradigm after "puṣa" is introduced in the Tibetan as lṛṭ, but the forms (pupoṣa and so on) and the parallel sections show it is liṭ; translated as liṭ. Likewise, for radha in luṅ the Tibetan cites "pug-anta" for the change of cli to aṅ, which is evidently a slip for "puṣādi"; translated accordingly. Here མདོས is the instrumental "by the sūtra," not the ritual thread-cross. This piece treats dhū, grah and śṝ in the kryādi class, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (halaḥ śnaḥ śānaj jhau, graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ, śṝdṝprāṃ hrasvo vā, vṝto vā, ṛcchatyṝtām, ṝta id dhātoḥ). In "in the ātmanepada" the Tibetan uses བདག, "self," as the short name of the ātmanepada endings, not the doctrinal self. The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example bhunāti and hūnīte for dhunāti and dhunīte, རང for taṅ, ལཊ for loṭ, ལིཊ for luṭ, ལིང for lṛṅ, gṛhvāni for gṛhṇāni, dhavihā for dhavitā), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The Tibetan does not write out the long vowels of the roots śṝ and dhū consistently; they are given here as the forms require.  This piece treats dṝ, pṝ, jyā, vrī, jñā and śranth in the kryādi class, citing Pāṇinian sūtras (śṝdṝprāṃ hrasvo vā, vṝto vā, ṛcchatyṝtām, ṝta id dhātoḥ, halaḥ, grahijyā..., jñājanor jā, vā 'nyasya saṃyogādeḥ). The root written བྲཱྀ, glossed "obstructing," is read as vrī (vrīñ varaṇe), as all its forms (avraiṣīt, vivrāya, vretā, vrīyāt) require; its present forms, written པྲྀ་ཎཱ་ཏི and the like, are given as vrīṇāti and so on. The benedictive of pṝ is given as the text has it, pīryāt; standard Pāṇinian grammar gives pūryāt. As before, the text keeps guṇa throughout the perfect of vrī. The Tibetan transliterations contain many slips (for example ལ་བ for laṅ, ཨ་ཥྟཱ་ས for abhyāsa, jijyītha, jijyaiva, abraiṣīt), and forms are given in their evident standard spelling. The last-person perfect of vrī lacks a dual in -iva as transmitted.  This passage of a Tibetan commentary on Pāṇini's grammar quotes Sanskrit sūtras and verb forms in Tibetan script; they are romanized exactly as spelled, including evident irregularities. The Tibetan "first person" (skyes bu dang po) follows the Indian order, in which the first person corresponds to the Western third person and the "last person" to the Western first. The Pāṇinian rules cited by their Tibetan renderings are translated in English. "ka 'gro ba" is rendered as kit, a suffix having k as its indicatory letter; "bal" is the class val; and "dbyangs don" is taken as "for the sake of the accent."  The Sanskrit forms and sūtras are romanized exactly as the Tibetan spells them, irregularities included. Pāṇinian rules cited by their Tibetan renderings are translated in English. "Becomes it" reads i ta for a ta, following the sense of the rule on the penultimate ṛ. The remark that "the operation as for san does not apply" refers to the reduplicated aorist of gaṇa, though here it stands after the benedictive forms. The person terms follow the Indian order, as before.  Sanskrit forms are transliterated letter for letter as spelled, and several carry evident slips that are kept, for example akathayitā with a stray augment in luṭ, aṃkayate and arthayeta in the parasmaipada optative where aṃkayet and arthayet are expected, aṃkāpayiti for aṃkāpayati, arthapayati for arthāpayati, āṃchikana with ch for c, and arthayiṣīlāstrāṃ for arthayiṣīyāstāṃ. The bracketed syllable rtha in arthayate is an editorial supply in the source.
The Tibetan a-taṅ and taṅ are the parasmaipada and ātmanepada endings respectively, and are rendered by those names.
The sentence "since the a has been elided, the operation that applies as when ṇic follows is not carried out" renders a garbled line (literally "a-ka byis pa", read as "a ka phyis pa", "the a of ka elided"); its exact sense is uncertain.
House glossary "being / destiny" for ’gro ba does not fit here: in the root gloss of aṃka it means "going," and in the phrase for the it-markers ñ and ṇ it renders the grammatical term it, literally "what goes away."
In the gloss of the puk sūtra, rīṅ is rendered "to hear" after the Tibetan nyan pa, a translation of śravaṇa where the Dhātupāṭha has sravaṇa, "to ooze"; the gloss of krūyī ends in an unclear syllable, so its sense is left as uncertain; the phrase "roots of their own that end in ā" reads a corrupt rang byings sā ta mgra’ can as ā mtha’ can.
"When ṇi follows aṃkā" reads the Tibetan i kā as aṃkā.
"The rule cited as pracad" renders an unclear phrase in the aṃka luṅ derivation; its reference is uncertain.
In the second artha commentary citation, ming dbyi is read as dbyi, "elided," matching the parallel aṃka citation.
Tibetan slips read by sense: brtod for brjod, "reduplicate"; ma ba rjong for mi brjod, "is not reduplicated"; lring for lṛṅ.
The closing Sanskrit line is a colophon to the section, evidently for iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sūtrāc curādayaḥ samāptāḥ; it is transliterated as spelled.  Sanskrit forms are transliterated letter for letter as spelled; many carry evident slips that are kept, for example kāryiṃti, kāriṃyarta, kārayotu and akārayiṃte where kārayati, kārayet, kārayatu and akārayat are expected, corayimyati for corayiṣyati, and uḍḍhaukanatāṃ for aḍuḍhaukatāṃ.
The sūtra cited as nāgopiśāspriditāṃ is evidently nāglopiśāsvṛditām; the Tibetan spelling ནཱ་གཱོ carries a stray ā-sign, which is dropped in the transliteration. The opening sūtra hetumaticāhetuḥ is given as spelled.
"The eight and the eighty endings" renders brgyad dang brgyad cu literally; the intended count is unclear, perhaps the eighteen personal endings.
House glossary "condition" for rkyen is set aside here: in this grammatical context it renders pratyaya in the sense of "suffix." Likewise ’gro ba in phrases such as "ṛ as their it" renders the grammatical term it, literally "what goes away," while in the root glosses of ḍhaukṛ and ṭuośvi it means "going."
"By the rule that, where ak has not been elided, the treatment is as with san when caṅ follows" reads the garbled ya bal tsang pha rol las na bzhin as the rule sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'nag lope.
"With r brought in" renders ra drangs pa; its exact sense is uncertain.
In the cur section, ལེཊ (leṭ) is kept as written though laṭ is evidently meant; "the rule beginning with what ends in puk" renders bu ka mtha’ sogs, evidently the rule pugantalaghūpadhasya ca.
In the ḍhaukṛ luṅ derivation a stray syllable group ḍhaḍa before ak is left untranslated, and the Tibetan reads tsa du for caṅ. "By giving in" in its lṛṭ line reads in as iṭ.
Tibetan slips read by sense: sman pa for smon pa, "benedictive"; ’grel pa ra for ’grel par, "the commentary"; tsī for tsli, "cli"; ŚĀ su ri for śāsu ṛ in the repeated sūtra gloss; lit for lṛṭ before corayimyati; bzhun for bzhin.

Sanskrit forms are transliterated letter for letter as spelled, with b or v for the Tibetan letter ba according to the evident word; many carry evident slips that are kept, for example śvūyeyitā for śvāyayitā, śrāyayiṣyati for śvāyayiṣyati, astamhayata for astambhayat, baryasīṣivatāṃ for paryasīṣivatām, sevayiṅhuti for sevayiṣyati, vyasīṣatata for vyasīṣahat and cakīsayatu for cakāsayatu. The root heads stamvū and the stems savi and unī are likewise given as spelled, for stambhu, sevi and undi.
The sūtra stambhusibusahāṃcadi is evidently stambhusivusahāṃ caṅi; the commentary citation subhātoranikācaścasanātkacidvā is evidently subdhātor anekācaś ca sanvat kvacid vā.
Glosses of roots are rendered from the Tibetan: skri ba pa in the stambhu heading is read as sgrib pa, "obstructing," matching the gloss that follows; for ṣivu, thags kyi rgyu is "the warp of a weave," setting aside the house rendering "cause" for rgyu; for cakāsṛ the Tibetan gives sgra smad pa, "a contemptible sound," a common noun here, so the name Kutsa used elsewhere for smad pa does not apply.
"Even though a prefix, the reason for changing s to ṣ, comes before" reads nyer bsgyur as upasarga, prefix; the stray syllables tsa na after it are left untranslated.
Tibetan slips read by sense: sa pra sār nar for samprasāraṇar; ’dies for ’dis; satsli and tsī for tsli, "cli"; ’os ngos for ’os; ni bcar for ṇi tsang; zung du for thung ngu, "shortened"; ṇi tsha for ṇi tsa, "ṇic"; lit, lring and līṭ for lṛṭ; u bangdhā for upadhā; and a repeated "on a light syllable" in the ṣaha derivation is given once. Sanskrit rules and examples are romanized as the Tibetan spells them, and the text's tense labels are kept even where they seem displaced (for example lṛṭ for liṭ in the sma rule, and liṅ for laṅ in the ha and śaśvat rule). The gloss "I do not go to the Kali age" reflects the Tibetan translator's rendering of Kaliṅga as rtsod ldan, the Age of Strife. The phrase rendered "the separate particles na and nu" is literally "the unexhausted na and nu." The gloss "done in the former time of Viṣṇu" (khyab bdag) and the gloss "I did it by turns" are uncertain in sense. Evident slips read in their obvious sense: མ་ཕྱོགས་པ as མགྱོགས་པ ("quickly"), རྵཱ་ཏུ as jātu, and ཀ་ཐི as katham. The gloss མ་གོས is read as མགོས, "with his head," and ཀྲཾཏ as kṛt. The glosses "Please protect my work" and "Come as you wish" (ཁྱོད་འདོད་པ་འབྱོད) are uncertain in sense. "Śūdra" renders དམངས་རིགས, the lowest of the four classes. Throughout the passage short glosses are interleaved with the running text, mostly giving the meaning of the forms just cited or about to be cited. They are kept in parentheses where they stand. The glosses "one who goes about at night" and "growth" in the first section seem to have strayed from the preceding discussion of rātri and from a word for vṛddhi. The glosses "a measure; good giver; wisdom; direct knowledge" match prastha (a measure), suda, prajña and abhijña. The glosses after the dadāti rule match limpa, vinda, dhāraya, pāraya, vedaya, udejaya, cetaya, sātaya and sāhaya. The glosses in the dunyor section match the ṇa forms listed just before them, with "frost" for avaśyāya. The glosses in the śilpini section belong to grāha and graha, and those in the prusṛlvaḥ section belong to hāyana. The one obscure gloss after the first grahaḥ could not be construed.
Evident slips in the forms, kept as written: in the limpa list, pedayaḥ stands for vedayaḥ and catayaḥ for cetayaḥ, and dhārayaḥ is missing. Jalaḥ stands for jvalaḥ, and pyādhaḥ for vyādhaḥ. Āśvābaḥ stands for āśrāvaḥ, and tajakaḥ for rajakaḥ. The first grahaḥ under vibhāṣā grahaḥ should be grāhaḥ, and bhūhiḥ stands for bhūtiḥ. The Tibetan writes ṇyut once for ṇyuṭ.
In the jvalādi section the end of the list is written kab; Pāṇini's list ends at kas. In the samabhihāra rule the text glosses samabhihāra as "equal doing," and this is rendered here as "repeated action." The rule cited as "not in the domain near where ś goes" is a literal rendering of the Tibetan for the rule that changes ec to ā in the root list, but not before a śit affix. The root khanu is glossed "destroying" in the text, and hṛñ "harming"; both are kept as written. Where the text says an affix's n "serves the vowel," the wording is kept; it seems to refer to the accent purpose of the marker.  As in the preceding passages, many short Tibetan glosses are interleaved with the running text. They are kept in parentheses where they stand. Most of them give the meaning of forms cited just before or just after them. "Prosperity" and "birth" refer to bhūti and sūta. The long list of "dwelling in..." glosses refers to the ṣṭha forms: the peg is śaṅku, the thumb aṅgu, madder mañji, the peacock barhi, and the gods divi. The holder list refers to śaktigraha and the rest. "Lies in the sky" and "lies on the chest" refer to khaśaya and udaraśaya. The fragment "spoken from the mouth; the supreme ear's ..." is garbled and its reference is unclear.
Several slips are kept as written. Yaṃtiḥ, baṃtiḥ and taṃtiḥ are written with anusvāra and b for yantiḥ, vantiḥ and tantiḥ. Sayiḥ stands for satiḥ, kanpaladaḥ for kambaladaḥ, daṭigrahaḥ for ghaṭīgrahaḥ, and baktragaḥ probably for vaktragaḥ. Samagaḥ stands for sāmagaḥ, sūrapaḥ for surāpaḥ, śidhupaḥ for śīdhupaḥ, and bidyāśaskaraḥ for vidyā yaśaskaraḥ. In the ṣṭha list, śaṅku and mañji have no form; amāṣṭhaḥ and āmāṣṭhaḥ stand for ambaṣṭhaḥ and āmbaṣṭhaḥ; and dvi and tri appear where the sūtra list has them. This piece continues the commentary on Pāṇini's third book (3.3.119 to 3.3.128 and vārttikas, then 3.4.18 and 3.4.21), followed by the rules on ktvā and lyap from books one, six and seven (1.2.7, 1.2.23 to 25, 6.4.31 and 32, 6.4.18, 6.4.38, 7.1.37, 7.2.51, 7.2.55 and 56, 7.4.43). Thus bracharaḥ and samubrachadaḥ stand for pracchadaḥ and samupacchādaḥ (the second should be long), ghukhābrājati for bhuktvā vrajati, alikhalāoḥpratiṣedhegdā for alaṃkhalvoḥ pratiṣedhe ktvā, kṣīskandasyandoḥ for na ktvi skandisyandoḥ, pūdaśca for pūṅaś ca, pālyapi for vā lyapi, and īkhatkaraḥ, īṣatvānaḥ and naṃṣṭrā for īṣatkaraḥ, īṣatpānaḥ and naṃṣṭvā. "Khvā," "khyā," "gtvā," "ghā" and "ktā" in the running text are scribal forms of the affix ktvā. "Niśa" stands for the root naś.

Interlinear glosses displaced from their words are given inline as "(gloss: ...)". Several sit far from the word they explain: "obtaining; going; debt; pervading" repeats the root meanings of vaha, vraja, vyaja and apa; "becomes slightly rich" and the like explain the āḍhyaṃbhava examples; "drinks a little; hard to drink; easy to drink" belong to īṣatpāna and the rest; "endured well" belongs to sumarṣaṇa; "makes ornament; makes certain" belong to alaṃkṛtvā and khalukṛtvā; "thirst," "patience" and "subtle" belong to tṛṣ, mṛṣ and kṛś; "having been cleansed; pure" and "Śiva" belong to pū. "Rich with joy" renders dga' ba as written; dka' ba, "with difficulty," is probably meant. "Drinks well" for sudharṣaṇa may be a slip for 'thub, "overcomes." Some glosses could not be identified and are given in phonetics: tserpa ('tsher pa), tsepa (tshes pa, said to be "from the sūtra"), nyepa (nyed pa) and tulga (tul ga).

Grammatical senses of glossary terms: ལས here is mostly the ablative "from," and in "agent and object" it means the grammatical object (karman), not karma. Glossed as "to go" or "going," འགྲོ་བ is a verb meaning. In "one whose k goes" (kit), "whose ū goes," "whose u goes" and "whose ut goes," it means an indicatory letter that drops away. དོན means "sense," as in "in the sense of an action." མཐའ means "final" or "end," not an extreme. ཡུལ appears only within spyod yul, "domain of activity," the gloss on gocara. དགའ་བ ("joy") and བཟོད་པ ("patience," "endured") appear in glosses. མདོ ("sūtra") appears in one gloss. དྲང་སྲོང is the sage Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa is cited in sūtra 1.2.25 as the authority for the optional rule. Rendered literally, the gloss says this is the name of the sun's father. The words "bears the name of one whose k goes" render the technical term kit. "Set form" renders nipātana. "Preverb" renders upasarga.  This piece completes the commentary on the kṛt section of the Pāṇinivyākaraṇa. It covers the rules on lyap (6.4.69, 6.4.56 and 57, 6.4.70, 6.1.41, 6.1.44) and on ṇamul and khamuñ (3.4.22 to 3.4.59, with Kāśikā-type supplements). It closes with a Sanskrit colophon and a verse, followed by a Tibetan rendering of the verse. As before, sūtras and examples are romanized exactly as spelled, errors included. For example, bhuktvābhuktvāprajati stands for bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati, cauraṃkāri for cauraṃkāram, svādukṛtvāphukte for svādu kṛtvā bhuṅkte, samūlabhātaṃ for samūlaghātaṃ, ratvānidhāyaṃ for ratnanidhāyaṃ, jībagrāhaṃ for jīvagrāhaṃ, and urcaicakṛtya for uccaiḥkṛtya. "Sra" stands for sva, and "ktrā" in the sūtra for ktvā. "Samprasāraṇa" is spelled samprasūraṇa once in the Tibetan. At sūtra 6.1.44 the explanation omits "optionally," which the sūtra requires. The text says "to rim pa ṣa," a slip for piṣa, and is rendered "to piṣa." Sūtra 3.4.59 actually concerns an unpleasant statement (ayathābhipreta), but the Tibetan explains it as "expressing delight," and it is translated as written. "Mēṅ, to harm" is the text's own gloss on the root of mayati.

Interlinear glosses are given inline as "(gloss: ...)". Many are displaced from the words they explain. "Goes having eaten and eaten" explains bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati. "Does the act of a thief" explains cauraṃkāram. "Having said 'Well done!', he praises" explains sādhu kṛtvā stauti. "He eats having done it otherwise," and the three like it, explain anyathākāraṃ and the rest. "He eats having obtained a living" explains jīvavedaṃ. "Grinds dry, fine, coarse" explains śuṣkapeṣaṃ and the rest; the verb theg is read as btags, "ground." "Seized with the hand" explains hastagrāhaṃ. "Holds firmly like a jewel" explains ratnanidhāyaṃ. "Having seized the staff" explains yaṣṭiṃgrāhaṃ. "Expressing delight, he raised it high" explains uccaiḥkṛtya. "Natural form; not made" goes with prakṛtya (prakṛti). "Self-victor" (rang rgyal ba, the usual word for a pratyekabuddha) is unplaced and is translated literally. One gloss could not be identified and is given in phonetics: rabtu jabpa (rab tu byab pa).

The Sanskrit colophon is corrupt. It would read iti pāṇinivyākaraṇasya sūtrāt kṛtādayaḥ samāptāḥ. The final verse is the closing verse of Rāmacandra's Prakriyākaumudī, roughly prakriyākaumudī seyaṃ rāmacandraprakāśitā, asadvacastamovṛttād ... ciram. Both are transliterated exactly as written. In the Tibetan verse, "the Very Clear" (rab byed shin tu gsal ba) renders the title Prakriyākaumudī, and "binds the last of untrue speech" translates the Tibetan literally; the Sanskrit speaks of the darkness of false speech.

Grammatical senses of glossary terms: རང་བཞིན here means a word's natural form (prakṛti), not inherent existence. ལས is mostly the ablative "from"; it means the grammatical object (karman) in "object word," and "act" or "deed" in the thief gloss. འགྲོ་བ means "going." དོན means "sense." མཐའ means "ending" in "ending in the third case." In the verse, mtha' ma means "the last." རྒྱུད appears in rab tu rgyud, "continuing on," and is not tantra. རྒྱལ་བ appears only within the gloss "self-victor." དགའ་བ means delight. དཔེ appears in dper brjod, "illustrative examples." མདོ is Pāṇini's sūtra text. བསྟན་བཅོས is "treatise." ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ is "verses." ལེགས་སོ is "Well done!"  This is the closing piece of the text: two benedictory Sanskrit verses with their Tibetan renderings, then the translator's colophon and his dedicatory verses. Both Sanskrit verses are corrupt, and they are transliterated exactly as written. They would read: ācāryaṃ pātu bhagavān śiṣyaṃ pātu vināyakaḥ, nirvighnaṃ syāc ca sarvatra pāṇinīyaprasādataḥ; and maṅgalaṃ lekhakānāṃ ca pāṭhakānāṃ ca maṅgalaṃ, maṅgalaṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ bhūmibhūpatimaṅgalaṃ. "The Guide" renders rnam par 'dren pa, the Tibetan for vināyaka. "Writers" reads 'dri pa as 'bri pa. In "the land and the lord of the land," ས means "earth" or "land," not a bodhisattva ground.

The colophon names the patron as the Fifth Dalai Lama, by his full religious name, and presents him as Padmapāṇi, that is, Avalokiteśvara. The epithet ཉིད་གསུམ་ལྡན is read as the usual "endowed with the three vows." The Tibetan spells the opening syllables of his name dag dbang, a slip for ngag dbang. In personal names, རྒྱ་མཚོ is given in phonetics (Gyatso), not as "ocean." The translator, Ngawang Phuntsok Lhundrub (also called Tsewang Rabten Dorje), worked under the paṇḍitas Balabhadra (spelled Palabhadra) and Gokulanātha Miśra, and based his notes on Rāmacandra's Prakriyākaumudī. "The Complete Explanation" (kun bshad) is an unidentified work. A zho is a Tibetan unit of weight for precious metals.

The dating uses Tibetan conventions. "Fire, sky, ocean" are symbolic numerals (3, 0 and 4), and the clause about ten sixty-year cycles appears garbled in the Tibetan. "Nachang" (rna 'phyang) appears to be the year named rnam 'phyang (Vilambin, the thirty-second year of the cycle), and "Kündén" (kun ldan) is a later cycle year, here an iron rat year. "Chutö" reads chu stong as chu stod, the month named after the lunar mansion Pūrvāṣāḍhā. "The third victory day" (rgyal ba, the Jayā lunar days) is the thirteenth day of the fortnight. "Bashé" (ba she) is an unidentified lunar mansion or yoga, given in phonetics. "Completed" renders sbyang ba, probably a slip for sbyar ba, "composed." The parenthetical note on detailed annotations interrupts the dating sentence in the Tibetan, and is kept where it stands.

The dedicatory verses embed the patron's name: Lord of Speech (Ngag dbang), excellent intelligence (blo bzang), ocean (rgya mtsho). "Twofold law" is the joint religious and secular system. "Sole father of the Ganges" is a poetic image for the Himalaya. The folio marker at the end of the input is omitted.

Glossary terms: ཆོས here means Dharma, as in "Dharma college." རྒྱལ་བ appears in "Victorious Lord" (rgyal dbang) and as the name of a lunar day. ལུང་བསྟན is a prophecy. ཟླ་བ means "month" or "moon" in the dates. Within the name of Caitra, ནག་པ་ཟླ་བ is kept as Caitra. མཁས་པ is the adjective "learned" here, not the example name Dakṣa used earlier in the text. བཟོད་པ means "bear patiently." དཔེ appears in dper brjod, "illustrative examples." ས is "land." The verses render དགེ་བ as "virtue," སེམས་ཅན as "sentient beings" and འགྲོ་བ as "beings."

Just as the Bodhi tree now standing at Bodh Gayā neither is nor is not the same tree beneath which the Buddha attained awakening, so too this stupa is intended as the next generation of stupa — dependently arising according to the conditions of its environment, and ceaselessly proclaiming the Dharma for the benefit of all sentient beings.
